summary: For ages 9-10, build the strategic judgement of choosing an efficient method and knowing when a shortcut beats the general algorithm — and when it fails. Learners read the numbers to route a multiplication (25×40 mentally as 25×4×10 vs 347×26 by long multiplication), estimate an angle then measure with a protractor to verify, and order fractions by benchmarking against 1/2 versus finding a common denominator. The key insight: a 1/2 benchmark is fast and sufficient when fractions fall on different sides of 1/2 (e.g. 3/8 below, 5/8 above), but cannot separate two fractions on the same side of 1/2 (e.g. the close pair 5/8 vs 4/7), where another method such as equivalent fractions or a common denominator is needed. Estimation and tools work together: estimate first, then measure to confirm or correct. Prize the justification of the choice as much as the answer, since competing methods reach the same order.
misconceptions: Long-multiplies friendly products like 25×40, missing the mental route
Relies on visual inspection for angles and skips the protractor check
Uses common denominators for every fraction comparison even when a benchmark settles it instantly — inefficient
Applies a benchmark to two close, same-side fractions (5/8 vs 4/7) where it cannot separate them, and guesses
Treats the protractor as replacing estimation rather than checking it

activities.title: Estimate then verify an angle
steps: Look at a drawn angle and state an estimate aloud, e.g. 'about 40°'.
Place a protractor on the angle and read the actual measure, e.g. 38°.
Compare the estimate with the measurement and say whether the estimate was close.
Explain why estimating first was not wasted even though you measured afterwards.
activities.insight: The eye gives a ballpark; the tool confirms or corrects it. Estimating first makes you more likely to catch a measuring slip, and measuring checks the estimate — the two work together rather than one replacing the other.

activities.title: Benchmark versus common denominator for ordering fractions
steps: Order 3/8, 1/2, 5/8 by comparing each to 1/2 (below, at, or above a half) and write the order.
Order the same three fractions by finding a common denominator, and check the two methods agree.
Compare how long each method took and say which was quicker here.
Now try to order 5/8 and 4/7: test whether the 'compare to a half' check separates them (both are above 1/2).
When the 1/2 benchmark cannot separate them, find a common denominator (or equivalent fractions) to order them exactly, e.g. 5/8 = 35/56 and 4/7 = 32/56, so 4/7 < 5/8.
State a rule for yourself about which method fits which fractions.
activities.insight: Benchmarking against 1/2 instantly sorts fractions that fall on different sides of a half, but when both fractions sit on the same side of 1/2 the 1/2 benchmark cannot separate them — then a common denominator earns its keep. The skill is matching the method to the fractions' features, not always using one method.

activities.title: Route the multiplication by reading the numbers
steps: Look at 25×40 and decide whether a mental method or long multiplication is quicker.
Compute 25×40 mentally, e.g. as 25×4×10 = 100×10 = 1000.
Look at 347×26 and decide on a method.
Compute 347×26 by long multiplication and show the partial products.
For each, say what feature of the numbers made you choose that method.
activities.insight: Friendly numbers (round factors, easy regroupings) invite a mental route; awkward multi-digit numbers call for the written algorithm. Reading the numbers before starting saves effort.

activities.title: Argue with a shortcut-happy partner
steps: Work with a partner (real or role-played) who benchmarks every fraction comparison and trusts the eye for every angle.
When the partner benchmarks 5/8 vs 4/7 and declares them 'about the same', supply the counter-case: both are above a half, so the 1/2 benchmark cannot order them.
Show the partner how a common denominator settles 5/8 vs 4/7 exactly (35/56 vs 32/56).
When the partner reads an angle from the eye alone, insist on a protractor check and explain why.
Give the partner two fraction pairs where benchmarking is smart and two where it is not.
activities.insight: Being able to say when a shortcut works and when the algorithm is required — and defending a verification step — shows genuine fit judgement rather than rote method use.

checkQuestion: To put 3/8, 1/2 and 5/8 in order, one child finds a common denominator for all three; another just says '3/8 is below a half, 5/8 is above, so it's 3/8, 1/2, 5/8'. Who chose the smarter method here, and why? Would your advice change for ordering 5/8 and 4/7?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for recognising the benchmark (compare to 1/2) is quicker and sufficient for 3/8, 1/2, 5/8, while 5/8 and 4/7 both sit above 1/2 and close together so the benchmark cannot separate them and a common denominator or equivalence is warranted — a judgement about which method fits which fractions.
